extracted.intended_audience: researchers, educators, and policymakers interested in applications and impacts of AI in education
extracted.subtask_description: A literature-review style synthesis assessing how AI has been applied to and impacted education, focusing on administration, instruction (teaching), and learning; includes methodological choices for searching and sampling literature and a taxonomy of technical components and uses of AI in education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: administration, instruction, and learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the study is limited to the application and effects of AI in administration, instruction, and learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This three-part framework (administration, instruction/teaching, learning) follows Chassignol et al. and is used as the organizing lens for assessment and synthesis of studies on AI in education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research design: qualitative literature review with thematic/content analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A qualitative research approach leveraging literature review as a research design and approach is used; thematic and content analysis is employed to identify recurring themes across texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A systematic or semi-systematic literature review (retrogressive approach) is appropriate for descriptive aims and ensures findings are evidence-backed by existing studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search strategy: keywords, databases, and journal quality threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Use keywords and search strings across databases such as EBSCOhost, ProQuest, Web of Science, and Google Scholar; include articles from journals with H-Index of 20 and above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search strings should be broad enough to capture relevant literature; applying a journal H-Index >= 20 is used here as a quality/reputation filter for inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and exclusion criteria for literature selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial selection of articles published after 2009 that match keywords and focus on the nature of AI and its impact on education; further exclusion based on relevance and quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference is given to studies focusing on the nature/impact of AI in education; quantitative studies were given preference in this review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling: sample size and eliminative process
rubrics_metrics.description: From an initial set (e.g., 250 articles) a further review narrows the corpus to a sample (30 articles) considered sufficient to inform conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an eliminative process based on relevance and quality metrics (e.g., H-Index) and favor studies that meet methodological preferences stated above.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI system model: learner model
rubrics_metrics.description: Learner model is established based on behaviour data generated from the learning process to analyze thinking and capability and assess learning abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learner modelling connects learning results to factors including materials, resources, and teaching behaviours and is critical for improving independent learning capabilities and tailoring instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI system model: knowledge model
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge model establishes a knowledge structure map with detailed learning contents, expert knowledge, rules of common mistakes and misunderstandings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge models support mapping of content and provide the basis for diagnosing misconceptions and structuring personalized learning paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI system model: teaching model
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching model determines rules to access the knowledge field and enables instructors or the system to tailor teaching strategies and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining learner and knowledge models, the teaching model operationalizes pedagogical rules and can be grounded in tutoring theories to provide interventions or hints.

rubrics_metrics.name: User interface and human–machine interaction requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: User interface should present learners' performance through multiple input media (voice, typing, clicks) and outputs (text, figures, cartoons); advanced HMI provides natural language interaction, speech recognition, and emotion detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multimodal interfaces facilitate richer interaction; emotion detection and NL interaction add affect-sensitivity and personalization capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core intelligent technology: machine learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine learning is the core of knowledge discovery, parsing training data to generate meaningful patterns; used for recommendations, grading (image recognition), and prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes algorithms and subfields such as decision trees, inductive logic programming, clustering, reinforcement learning, Bayesian networks, and deep neural networks (deep learning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Core intelligent technology: learning analytics
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning analytics focuses on data from student characteristics and knowledge objects to tailor educational methods, provide feedback, and generate early warning systems for at-risk students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning analytics uses ML, data visualization, learning sciences, and semantics; challenge is to extend from measurable cognitive outcomes to interpersonal and creative competencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core intelligent technology: educational data mining
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational data mining discovers association rules and builds predictive models to extract hidden knowledge from learner data, enabling automated responses and personalized learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data mining can predict future performance from limited inputs (e.g., few assignments) and support curriculum adjustments and personalized learning pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional goal: personalization and adaptive instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: AI systems should customize curriculum and content to individual students' needs and abilities, improving uptake, retention, and the quality of learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptive and intelligent web-based educational systems (AIWBES), ITS, and ILEs are concrete implementations; personalization can include competency-based learning and tailored content paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional goal: automation of administrative tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: AI should automate administrative functions such as reviewing student work, grading, plagiarism detection, and management to improve efficiency for instructors and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automation can free teacher time for higher-level pedagogical tasks, but systems must be validated for reliability and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional goal: intelligent tutoring and interactive learning environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems such as interactive learning environments (ILEs) and intelligent tutoring systems (e.g., ACTIVE Math, MATHia) provide feedback, manage performance, and support instruction across subjects and levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These systems integrate learner modelling, content models, and pedagogical strategies to scaffold problem solving and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of robotics and cobots as instructional tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedded systems and humanoid robots (cobots) may function as tutors or colleague-robots to teach routine tasks, support pronunciation/spelling practice, and promote self-regulated learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research compares humanoid tutors to human tutors; robot tutors can vary in social-supportive behaviour and have been studied for long-term support of self-regulation in primary school children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of immersive technologies (VR/3-D/gaming) for experiential learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtual reality and 3-D technologies enable simulation and experiential learning opportunities beyond physical classrooms, supporting practical skill development and engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: VR supports scenario-based learning and can integrate with AI to create global classrooms and simulated professional experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics for AI impact in education
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess AI's impact on education using metrics such as improved efficiency, instructional effectiveness, personalized learning outcomes, global access, and quality of learner experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies should measure learning gains, retention, teacher efficiency, accessibility improvements, and whether AI-enabled tools produce measurable pedagogical improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity and ethical risk: academic integrity and cheating
rubrics_metrics.description: AI introduces risks such as degradation of academic integrity and new cheating vectors (e.g., paper mills and automated content generation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigation includes proctoring, clear consequences, institutional policy, and design of AI tools that discourage misuse; policymakers and institutions must consider integrity-preserving measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical deployment constraints for mobile AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Running ML on mobile devices requires efficient execution platforms (e.g., Snapdragon Neural Processing Engine, HiAI, Android Neural Networks API) and mobile-optimized models (SqueezeNet, MobileNet, ShuffleNet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mobile deployment reduces latency and dependency on servers, enabling interactive and personalized learning on-device; model and platform choice affect responsiveness and feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desired future capabilities: creativity, affect-sensitivity, and initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Future desirable AI systems should shape students' imagination and creativity, analyze learning style and emotional condition, and stimulate subjective initiative to improve creativity and learning capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This suggests moving beyond rule-based personalization to systems that support higher-order skills and affective dimensions of learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement challenge: assessing complex competencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning analytics currently faces difficulty measuring complex competencies (interpersonal skills, arts, literature) which pose a new level of complexity for assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research and tool design must address measurement validity and generalizability across contexts while balancing specificity and cross-course applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling requirement: build data maps and association rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Models should help build data maps and association rules from collected educational data to improve learning by establishing structures and relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong modelling layer (learner/knowledge/teaching models) is core to AI systems; technologies supply computational power but models are necessary to make data-driven pedagogical decisions.
